subject: Agriculture
title: The Broiler Revolution
description: A fast breakdown of The Broiler Revolution for builders.

hook.text: In 1950, a chicken took 84 days to reach market weight. Today it takes 42 days—half the time.

buildup.text: After World War II, breeders competed in 'Chicken of Tomorrow' contests to create the meatiest, fastest bird.

discovery.text: Selective breeding, not drugs, drove most of the change. Modern broilers gain weight four times faster than 1950s birds.

twist.text: These birds grow so fast their legs sometimes can't support them. Heart failure is common in broilers.

climax.text: Chicken is now the world's cheapest meat protein—feeding billions but raising welfare questions.

punchline.text: We built a bird optimized for growth, not for living.

quiz.question: How long does a modern broiler chicken take to reach market weight?

details.summary: The broiler revolution transformed chicken from an expensive luxury into the world's cheapest meat in just 60 years through intensive breeding, industrial housing, and vertical integration. This topic covers the science, economics, and welfare implications.
details.whyItMatters: Modern broilers reach slaughter weight in just 6 weeks—four times faster than 1950s chickens. This efficiency feeds billions of people cheaply but raises serious concerns about animal welfare and antibiotic use.
takeaways: Broiler chickens reach market weight of 2.5 kg in about 42 days, down from 112 days in 1957
The Chicken of Tomorrow contest in 1948 launched the modern broiler industry
Fast growth rates cause leg problems and heart failure in a significant percentage of birds

faq.question: How did broiler chickens get so big so fast?
faq.answer: Decades of selective breeding for rapid growth, combined with optimized nutrition, controlled environments, and antibiotics, shortened the growth period from over 100 days to about 42 days. Modern broilers grow roughly four times faster than 1950s birds.

faq.question: What are the welfare concerns with modern broiler chickens?
faq.answer: Rapid growth rates cause skeletal problems, heart failure, and difficulty walking in many birds. Dense housing in windowless sheds limits natural behaviors. Slow-growing breeds and higher welfare standards are increasingly demanded by consumers.
